The two ATH-002 encoded-PowerShell detections are not isolated events but a single scripted burst: both fire on the same host/account with identical evasion characteristics (base64 payload, -NoProfile, hidden window) only ~99 seconds apart, indicating automated or operator-driven repetition of the same tradecraft rather than two independent user actions.

The MEDIUM-severity encoded PowerShell activity on desktop-4pvps6e should be re-scored upward because the same host is the origin of 589,476 outbound connections, of which 329,448 are attributed to powershell.exe reaching a single destination (192.168.47.136) — i.e., the interpreter flagged for obfuscated execution is also the top network talker on the box.

The base64 payload that 'does not obviously fetch remote code' is likely an in-memory stager or beacon loader whose network egress occurs after decoding, which would explain why static command-line inspection found no remote fetch while powershell.exe subsequently generated hundreds of thousands of connections to 192.168.47.136.

The processes named beacon.exe and beacon2.exe communicating with 192.168.137.129, 192.168.182.128 and 192.168.253.129 are command-and-control implants (naming and multi-destination fan-out are consistent with a Cobalt-Strike-style framework), making the flagged PowerShell the likely delivery or hands-on-keyboard tooling stage of the same intrusion.

Outbound network activity attributed to lsass.exe (6,283 connections to 10.10.117.128) is anomalous for a legitimate LSASS process and suggests process injection into, or masquerading as, lsass.exe for credential access — a plausible next stage following the SYSTEM-context PowerShell execution on the same host.

The account context ties the detections to already-elevated access rather than an intrusion attempt: 'system' shows 4,458 successful authentications and zero failures with no resolvable source, so the obfuscated PowerShell represents post-compromise execution at the highest local privilege, not credential guessing or lateral entry into this host.

The security service stop on desktop-4pvps6e (ATH-012 / T1685) and the sustained beacon.exe outbound traffic to 192.168.137.129, 192.168.182.128 and 192.168.253.129 originate from the same host, so the defense-impairment event is best read as an enabling step within an already-active implant session rather than an isolated administrative action.

lsass.exe generating 6283 outbound network connections to 10.10.117.128 is anomalous: the Local Security Authority process does not normally initiate sustained egress to an arbitrary internal host, which is consistent with process injection into or masquerading as lsass.exe for credential-access and C2 purposes.

The case is scoped far too narrowly: the timeline covers a single second (2022-11-19T19:12:55Z) and one cited event, while the same host carries 589,476 outbound connections and 4,458 'system' authentications that are not represented in the case window, meaning the investigation is anchored on a symptom rather than the intrusion itself.

The 'system' account is the common pivot between the two datasets: it is the actor that stopped the security service and also the sole account behind 4,458 successful, zero-failed authentications on desktop-4pvps6e, so attacker actions on this host are running with SYSTEM-level privilege rather than an ordinary user context.

The coexistence of beacon.exe and beacon2.exe talking to three different destinations suggests deliberate C2 redundancy (primary plus fallback implant), a pattern typical of a framework-based intrusion where the operator provisions a second channel before impairing defenses.

powershell.exe accounting for 329,448 connections to a single destination (192.168.47.136) is more consistent with a scripted beaconing or data-transfer loop than with interactive administration; this channel is a candidate staging or exfiltration path and should be triaged ahead of the ATH-012 finding.
